extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, legal historians, law students, and policy makers interested in the history and legitimacy of notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Historical and evaluative analysis of notice-and-comment (informal) rulemaking in U.S. administrative law, tracing its English origins and the procedural components that bear on its legitimacy and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice, comment, and final-rule publication (Section 553 components)
rubrics_metrics.description: The core procedural trio requiring agencies to publicize proposed regulations, solicit public comments, and issue/publish final rules (the first two recommendations of the AG’s Committee minority and the third requirement to issue final rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the central procedural cocktail that became Section 553 of the APA (codified at 5 U.S.C. §553). The article links these components to the AG’s Committee’s minority recommendations and to the 1935 Federal Register Act’s publication requirement. These three duties together form the minimal formal structure of American informal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation and fairness as purposes of notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment exists ‘to reintroduce public participation and fairness to affected parties’ and to ensure agencies ‘have before it the facts and information relevant to a particular administrative problem, as well as suggestions for alternative solutions.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting judicial and scholarly statements (e.g., Batterton v. Marshall; Guardian Fed. Sav. & Loan; Am. Hosp. Ass’n v. Bowen), the article presents public participation and fairness as twin justificatory aims that are often invoked to evaluate the legitimacy of a rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational function: gathering facts and alternative solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment is evaluated on its ability to provide agencies with facts and suggestions for alternative solutions relevant to the problem being regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars describe this as the primary practical benefit of participation — educating agencies and improving rules. Evaluations should ask whether the procedure meaningfully improved the agency's factual record or choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative/democratic desiderata (participatory, representative, deliberative, transparent, egalitarian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking has been praised as participatory, representative, deliberative, transparent, and relatively egalitarian; these qualities are used as normative metrics for assessing its legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites scholarship celebrating these traits (Farina et al., Asimow, Seidenfeld, Eskridge & Ferejohn). Evaluations of rulemaking often measure to what extent the process realized these democratic ideals in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency responsiveness to comments (must address 'comments which are of cogent materiality')
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are obliged to respond to comments that are of 'cogent materiality'; courts have at times invalidated rules when agencies failed to respond adequately, though other decisions have signaled a more minimal 'check-the-box' approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case citations: United States v. Nova Scotia Food Prods. Corp., 568 F.2d 240 (2d Cir. 1977) (cogent materiality standard); Ohio v. EPA, 603 U.S. 279 (2024) (recent example of invalidation for inadequate engagement); Little Sisters of the Poor, 591 U.S. 657 (2020) (Court's tendency to accept nominal opportunities for participation). Evaluators should look at both the substance of agency responses and whether courts treat those responses as meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication requirement (Federal Register / public notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finalized regulations must be published (the 1935 Federal Register Act required publication and inspired the APA’s publication obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication in the Federal Register (modeled on England’s Rules Publication Act 1893) is both a formal legal requirement and a transparency measure; compliance is a basic metric of procedural regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with entities likely to be affected
rubrics_metrics.description: English Rules Publication Act 1893 (and related reforms) required administrative bodies to publicize proposals and consult with entities likely to be affected by the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes consultation as distinct from open notice: consultations help gather information and secure assent from interest groups. Evaluations of rulemaking should distinguish broad public notice from targeted consultations and assess whether consultations were meaningfully conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laying procedures / legislative oversight (legislative veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: English laying procedures required Parliament an opportunity to approve or reject delegated legislation via 'laying procedures'; this legislative veto was considered critical in England for securing democratic legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence or absence of a legislative veto/laying mechanism is presented as an important metric of democratic legitimacy. The article documents that Americans considered but ultimately rejected laying procedures; assessing legitimacy may involve asking whether legislative oversight mechanisms exist and how effective they are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and closure of procedural loopholes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms (e.g., Donoughmore Committee recommendations) sought to eliminate loopholes and standardize and expand consultation, laying, and publication requirements governing delegated legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One way to evaluate procedural quality is to examine whether requirements are comprehensive and uniformly applied or whether loopholes permit agencies to evade participatory safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transsubstantive application / uniform administrative procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural requirements should apply transsubstantively (across the wide swath of federal agencies) rather than in piecemeal fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AG’s Committee’s inductive study and the APA aimed for uniform administrative procedural requirements. Evaluations should consider whether a rulemaking regime is applied consistently across agencies or varies by subject matter or agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of English procedural transplant to U.S. constitutional structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether English-style laying procedures and other transplanted mechanisms are compatible with U.S. separation-of-powers and the practical behavior of U.S. legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article identifies reasons the U.S. did not import laying procedures: perceived lack of utility (legislators' lack of desire to interfere), structural differences between parliamentary and separation-of-powers systems, and the decline of the nondelegation doctrine. Evaluations of transplant proposals should analyze institutional fit and likely political behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial transplantation and its legitimacy consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans imported the 'notice' and 'comment' dimensions of English procedure but declined to import the legislative veto; the partial transplantation itself is a factor in debates about notice-and-comment’s legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames 'partial transplantation' as potentially fateful: it produced the American form of informal rulemaking but may help explain perennial legitimacy critiques. Assessments of reform proposals should consider whether completing the transplantation (e.g., adding laying procedures) would improve legitimacy or create new constitutional problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusiveness and distributional effects (barriers to participation; bias toward business; administrative subordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations consider whether the notice-and-comment process is genuinely inclusive or whether barriers and interest-group dynamics (e.g., disproportionate business influence) skew outcomes and subordinate vulnerable people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites scholarship documenting low levels of public comments, business advantages, and agency behaviors that subordinate marginalized interests (e.g., Yackee & Yackee; Sant’Ambrogio & Staszewski; Bijal Shah). Assessments should measure who participates, whose views are reflected, and whether the process equalizes or amplifies certain interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textualist/fair-notice vs. participatory interpretation of Section 553
rubrics_metrics.description: Some judicial/textualist accounts view the object of notice-and-comment as 'fair notice' rather than as a vehicle for meaningful public participation; this interpretive stance is a metric affecting how strictly courts enforce participatory substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references Hickman & Thomson and Little Sisters of the Poor to show that if courts treat the statute as focusing on notice (fair notice) rather than the participatory quality of comments, then procedural compliance may be assessed more narrowly. Evaluators should note the interpretive lens courts apply when reviewing procedural adequacy.
